found.title: Is the selector already published under another name?
found.answer:
I found no paper that does claim 1. Nothing I opened runs a per-report selector that judges each coder by how many training reports the code it proposed has, after all coders have answered, with the selector frozen on one year and tested on later years. The main gaps remain the ones the first round named: hundreds of codes, per-code base-rate measurement, and the frozen later-year test. That is still not proof that nobody has done it. OpenAlex was blocked for the whole session, Semantic Scholar search mostly failed, and arXiv rate-limited often.

EnergyRoute (full text read) is still the closest paper. Here is precisely what it does:
- **Routing signal:** the Helmholtz free energy of the encoder's logits, computed before any LLM call.
- **Thresholds:** the 40th and 80th percentiles of energy, computed on the incoming test batch itself.
- **Combining:** it fuses rather than selects. Tier 2 mixes in a retrieved-neighbour (kNN) distribution in log space, and Tier 3 averages encoder and LLM probabilities 50/50 over the top 5.
- **Proposed-label features:** none. No property of the proposed label, such as its frequency or per-class accuracy, enters the routing.
- **Split:** temporal, which corrects the first-round critic (it had found no split statement). Training is 2018-2020 (82,316 projects); the test is only 500 stratified projects from 2021, under 2 per class across 301 classes.
- **Frequency groups:** head (top 20% by training frequency), mid (middle 60%) and tail (bottom 20%). Tail micro-F1 rises from 0.333 to 0.583; head gains 0.9 points and mid 2.9 points. Macro-F1 goes from 0.738 to 0.778, against 0.701 for a FrugalGPT cascade. On Web of Science it goes from 0.770 to 0.804 (cascade 0.758).
- **Zero-shot LLM:** essentially useless on its task (micro-F1 0.002 with GPT-OSS-20B).
- **Citations:** Europe PMC lists no citing works. It cites FrugalGPT, RouteLLM, Hybrid LLM and energy-based out-of-distribution detection, and none of the newer LLM-vs-encoder deferral papers. The draft's references.bib and manuscript.tex do not cite it.

New partial precedents:
- **STREAQ (EMNLP Industry 2025):** routes to the large model when the small model's answer is the rare 'answer of interest'. That is a routing rule keyed on the rarity of the proposed label, which our selector also uses, but each question it routes has only two possible answers.
- **Arora et al. (EMNLP Industry 2024):** routes from SetFit to an LLM on Monte Carlo dropout variance, over 8-59 intents.
- **AspectBench (Front AI 2026):** learning-to-defer with several fine-tuned experts, stackers and confidence-gated LLM deferral, on 3-class sentiment.
- **Amazon Dual-Expert (2024):** the encoder proposes the top K candidates and the LLM picks one.
- **MILD (Cortes, Mao, Mohri, Zhong 2026):** theory for deferral when one expert is right far more often than the others; it is about the experts, not about rare classes.

Every published router I opened decides from the encoder's uncertainty or the input text, usually before the LLM answers. Several report results by frequency group, so that part is no longer new.

What remains new in claim 1, and narrowly:
1. The decision uses a property of each proposed answer, the training support of the code each coder named, and is made after all three coders have answered.
2. It selects one coder's answer instead of fusing, among three coders that include two LLM variants.
3. It is frozen on the training year and evaluated over a whole later year at natural proportions, on two datasets and with three LLMs.
4. It is compared head to head with confidence and energy routing.

Two caveats. The classic Local Class Accuracy and behaviour-knowledge-space methods already judge a classifier by the class it outputs. STREAQ already routes on proposed-label rarity in a binary setting. So the contribution should be stated as an increment, and the paper should show that training support adds something beyond a per-code precision table and beyond energy routing.

works.citation: Jang G, Kim MW, Nam Y, Yong Y, Lee KH, Lim C. EnergyRoute: energy-based uncertainty routing for selective retrieval and LLM assistance in hierarchical classification of biotechnology R&D projects. Sci Rep 16:19697 (2026). doi 10.1038/s41598-026-49886-1
works.what_they_did:
Routing method:
- KLUE-RoBERTa-large encoder; the Helmholtz free energy of its logits is the routing signal, computed before any LLM call.
- Thresholds are the 40th and 80th energy percentiles of the test batch.
- Tier 1 accepts the encoder's answer. Tier 2 fuses a 20-neighbour hybrid BM25/E5 kNN distribution in log space (lambda 0.7). Tier 3 sends 20% of items to GPT-OSS-20B with retrieved evidence, backfilled from the parent category for tail classes, then averages encoder and LLM 50/50 over the top 5.

Data and split:
- 301 leaf classes with a 964x imbalance.
- Train 2018-2020 (82,316); test 500 stratified items from 2021; WoS (142 classes, random benchmark split) as a second dataset.

Results:
- Macro-F1 0.738 to 0.778; FrugalGPT cascade 0.701.
- Head/mid/tail = top 20/middle 60/bottom 20% by training frequency: tail micro-F1 0.333 to 0.583, head +0.9 points, mid +2.9 points.
- Zero-shot GPT-OSS-20B micro-F1 0.002.
works.bearing:
Takes:
- 'encoder + retrieval + LLM routing beats the encoder and a confidence cascade on hundreds of imbalanced classes, with gains largest in the tail'
- 'temporal test year' as a novelty point. It is temporal, but the test is only 500 stratified items, not a natural-proportion year.

Leaves open:
- choosing after the answers
- any feature of the proposed label (none used)
- selection rather than fusion
- a selector frozen on training data (its thresholds come from the test batch)
- natural-proportion evaluation and multiple LLMs.

Must be the main head-to-head baseline and must be cited; it is not in references.bib.

works.citation: Sood P, Agrawal R, Sati M, George C, Ingle D. STREAQ: Selective Tiered Routing for Effective and Affordable Contact Center Quality Assurance. EMNLP 2025 Industry Track, pp. 1711-1726
works.what_they_did:
Two-tier routing:
- A fine-tuned phi-3-mini answers QA questionnaire items about call transcripts.
- Items whose small-model answer is the rare 'answer of interest' (minority label) are routed to a large LLM; a fine-tuned RoBERTa router, trained on whether the small model was right, is also used.
- Reports a 48% cost cut while keeping 88.9% of full-model precision on the rare answer.
works.bearing:
Takes:
- the narrow idea that the rarity of the proposed label is a routing trigger.

Leaves open:
- the multi-class setting (each question it routes has only two possible answers)
- training-support counts over hundreds of codes
- selection among three coders after all have answered
- frozen later-year test.

Should be cited as the closest instance of label-dependent routing.

works.citation: L2D-Clinical: Learning to Defer for Adaptive Model Selection in Clinical Text Classification. arXiv 2604.13285 (2026)
works.what_they_did:
Deferral model:
- Logistic regression (balanced weights) over BERT confidence, entropy and margin plus text length and keyword features; decides before the LLM is queried.

Tasks and split:
- ADE (binary) and MIMIC-IV treatment outcomes (3 classes).
- Random 70/15/15 and 80/10/10 splits.

Comparisons:
- Fixed confidence-threshold, random and oracle deferral.
- MIMIC F1: 0.980 vs 0.887 for BERT.

No per-frequency analysis.
works.bearing:
Takes:
- 'a logistic model decides per item between encoder and LLM'.

Leaves open:
- proposed-label features (none)
- post-answer decision
- many classes
- temporal test.

works.citation: Arora G, Jain S, Merugu S. Intent Detection in the Age of LLMs. EMNLP 2024 Industry Track. arXiv 2410.01627
works.what_they_did:
Hybrid routing:
- SetFit runs first; Monte Carlo dropout variance (M samples) flags uncertain queries, which go to an LLM (Claude 3 Haiku, Mistral Large).

Data:
- 8-59 intents.

Result:
- Hybrid within about 2% of LLM accuracy at about half the latency.
works.bearing: Industry precedent for uncertainty routing from a small model to an LLM; no per-intent frequency features, no post-answer selection, no temporal split. Does not take claim 1.

works.citation: Evaluating fine-tuned, embedding-based, and zero-shot models for aspect-based sentiment analysis in South Slavic news (AspectBench). Front Artif Intell 2026, doi 10.3389/frai.2026.1844418
works.what_they_did:
Learning-to-defer experiments for 3-class entity sentiment:
- Several fine-tuned PLM experts combined by majority vote, probability averaging, confidence pick and linear/random-forest stackers.
- Complete LLM deferral (the LLM sees the expert's label and probabilities and keeps or revises it).
- Confidence-gated selective LLM deferral.

Result:
- Supervised experts remain best.
works.bearing:
Takes:
- 'stacking / multi-expert deferral over fine-tuned models plus an LLM' in general.

Leaves open:
- 3 classes only
- no label-frequency feature
- no frequency bins.

Cites Montreuil 2026 and Kondadadi and Ortega 2026.

works.citation: Cheng et al. E-Commerce Product Categorization with LLM-based Dual-Expert Classification Paradigm. CustomNLP4U workshop 2024 (Amazon)
works.what_they_did: A fine-tuned domain expert proposes the top-K categories; an LLM chooses among them.
works.bearing: Filter-then-rerank family, already covered in the draft; no per-item choice between coders' final answers, no frequency feature. Does not take claim 1.

works.citation: Cortes C, Mao A, Mohri M, Zhong Y. Optimized Deferral for Imbalanced Settings (MILD). arXiv 2604.27723 (2026)
works.what_they_did: Two-stage learning-to-defer theory and algorithms for 'expert imbalance', where the router favours the expert that is most often right. Tested on image classification and LLM routing.
works.bearing: Theory reference for why a router can fall back on the majority expert. The imbalance is across experts, not classes; it uses no class-support features. Does not take claim 1.

works.citation: Montreuil Y et al. Learning-to-Defer with Expert-Conditioned Advice. arXiv 2603.14324 (2026)
works.what_they_did: Learning-to-defer that jointly picks an expert and the advice it receives, with consistency guarantees.
works.bearing: Not close; no classification-coding setting, no label-frequency features.

works.citation: Schlee M et al. LabelFusion: Fusing LLMs with Transformer Encoders for Robust Financial News Classification. arXiv 2512.10793
works.what_they_did: An MLP fuses the output of a prompted LLM with RoBERTa embeddings on a 10-class multi-label Reuters subset. Macro-F1: fusion 96.0, RoBERTa 94.6, LLM 93.9.
works.bearing: A fusion stacker, not a selector; only 10 classes; no frequency features. Already in the first round.

works.citation: Agarwal R et al. MADE: A Living Benchmark for Multi-Label Text Classification with UQ of Medical Device Adverse Events. ACL 2026 (arXiv 2604.15203)
works.what_they_did: Builds a temporally split, long-tailed hierarchical multi-label benchmark from device adverse-event reports and benchmarks over 20 encoder and decoder models. Small fine-tuned decoders are best from head to tail; reasoning LLMs help rare labels.
works.bearing: No selector, so it does not take claim 1. It is already cited in the project's notes as made2026. Relevant to claim 2's direction.

works.citation: Martin, Feng & Peng. Comparing LLM and Fine-Tuned Model Performance on NVDRS Circumstance Extraction. IEEE ICHI 2026, arXiv 2605.21845
works.what_they_did: A hybrid approach beats RoBERTa on all 15 circumstances with fewer than 5,000 positive training instances; the largest gains are on the rarest labels.
works.bearing: Claim 2, not claim 1. Its hybrid is assigned per label (static), not per report from the coders' answers.

now_taken: Routing between a fine-tuned encoder, kNN/retrieval and an LLM over about 300 imbalanced classes, reported by head/mid/tail frequency groups, beating a confidence cascade by a similar macro-F1 margin (+0.04): EnergyRoute, full text read.

'Tested on a later year' alone is not new for this design: EnergyRoute trains on 2018-2020 and tests on 2021 (500 stratified items), as does Emer (patents). What remains is a whole later year at natural proportions, with the selector frozen.

Using the rarity of the label a model proposed as a routing trigger: STREAQ (EMNLP Industry 2025) routes the small model's minority-label answers to a large LLM, in a setting where each question has only two possible answers.

Learning-to-defer / stacking over several fine-tuned experts plus an LLM, including majority vote, confidence pick and stacker baselines: AspectBench (Front AI 2026), L2D-Clinical, Arora et al. EMNLP Industry 2024.
Judging a classifier by the class it outputs: Local Class Accuracy and behaviour-knowledge-space methods (first round). So 'training support has no counterpart' must be softened.
still_open: A selector that chooses among three coders' final answers (encoder, zero-shot LLM, retrieval LLM) per report, after all have answered, using the training support of each proposed code. No paper I opened does this. Every published router I opened (EnergyRoute, L2D-Clinical, Arora, CMBS, TRACER, Emer) decides from the encoder's uncertainty or the input text before the LLM answers, or fuses the outputs. Searched with about 45 distinct queries over WebSearch (10), arXiv (about 25), Europe PMC (10), Crossref (9) and Semantic Scholar (1 of about 9 succeeded); OpenAlex was blocked for the whole session, so citation chasing was limited.

A selector frozen on one training year and evaluated over a whole later year at natural proportions, on two datasets and with three LLMs. Not found. EnergyRoute's thresholds are computed from the test batch, and its test is stratified (500 items).
Whether training support adds anything over a per-code precision (LCA/BKS) table and over EnergyRoute-style energy gating. This is an experiment, not a search; no paper runs this comparison.

Industry venues: one KDD ADS / SIGIR eCom / CIKM applied paper surfaced (CIKM 2026 web-page classification, which is not a selector). The ACL Anthology and KDD proceedings were not searched directly beyond WebSearch, so this was a shallow search.
Korean-language sources: not searched.

found.title: LLMs for tail labels and rare categories
found.answer:
Claim 2 is more fully taken than the first round thought, and on our own data source. MADE (Agarwal et al., ACL 2026 Main, arXiv 2604.15203; full text read) is a benchmark built from FDA medical-device adverse event reports via openFDA. Its labels are FDA problem terms mapped to IMDRF codes: 1,154 labels, multi-label, with ancestors added. It uses a strict temporal split (train 2015-2023, validation Jan-Jun 2024, test Jul 2024-Jun 2025) and reports macro-F1 by training-frequency bin (head >1%, medium, tail, extreme tail <0.01%). More than 20 models are compared: discriminatively and generatively fine-tuned Llama 1B-70B (LoRA and full), Ettin encoders, and prompted LLMs given 10 kNN-retrieved training examples, which is our retrieval coder. GPT-5 roughly doubles the best fine-tuned model on the extreme tail (0.34 vs 0.16), ties it on the tail (0.53) and loses on the head (0.68 vs 0.74). Even the fine-tuned 70B model stays at 0.16 on the extreme tail. That backs our 'a tuned LLM does not close the gap' result but means it is no longer new. Emer et al. (patents) and Martin/Feng/Peng (NVDRS) repeat the same split in other domains.
Two parts of claim 2 still look open. First, I found no study that sweeps the training size of a fine-tuned model against a fixed LLM and reports the result by class-frequency bin. Generic sweeps exist only in aggregate (Bucher & Martini: RoBERTa-large passes zero-shot BART above about 200 examples; few classes; no per-class bins). Second, our 1-5 training-report bin falls outside MADE's 5-occurrence minimum. The 'LoRA does not close the gap' point is also contested elsewhere: LoRA-tuned generators beat fine-tuned baselines on rare tags in FLAN-FinXC and on long-tailed events in Al Monsur et al. (EACL-F 2026), so it should be stated as a finding for our data, not a general rule.
On precision of LLM tail predictions on an unbalanced stream: I found nobody who reports it. MADE reports only macro-F1, Jaccard and uncertainty measures, with no precision/recall split and no false-positive analysis. It also scores on a 'truncated, stratified' 10,288-report test subset after HDBSCAN downsampling that keeps rare labels, so its rare-label scores are not at natural prevalence. This makes MADE a ready, citable example for our 'stratified tests overstate rare-code precision' point; I could not confirm exactly how its stratification was done. MADE has no routing, selection or ensemble across models. The XMC-with-LLM literature (ICXML, Infer-Retrieve-Rank, LLM-as-teacher tagging, ViXML) reports ranking metrics on public benchmarks, and in the abstracts and snippets I saw there were no per-frequency LLM-vs-fine-tuned results and no precision at natural prevalence. The rare-category-discovery search turned up only pre-LLM stream work and LLM false-positive filters.
Net effect: the draft must cite and position against MADE as the closest prior work for claim 2 and for the MAUDE setting (it is also a public CC0 temporal benchmark that reviewers may ask us to run on). Claim 3's natural-prevalence measurement and the selector of claim 1 are not touched by anything I found in this literature.

works.citation: Agarwal R, Wenzel M, Baur S, Zimmer J, Harvey G, Ma J. MADE: A Living Benchmark for Multi-Label Text Classification with Uncertainty Quantification of Medical Device Adverse Events. ACL 2026 (Main); arXiv 2604.15203 (Apr 2026)
works.what_they_did: openFDA device adverse event reports, FDA problem terms mapped to IMDRF codes (1,154 labels over 3 levels, about 8.8 per report, at least 5 occurrences each). Train 2015-2023, validation H1 2024, test Jul 2024-Jun 2025; evaluated on a truncated stratified test subset of 10,288. Discriminative and generative fine-tuning of Llama 1B-70B and Ettin (LoRA vs full), prompting of many open and API LLMs with 10 kNN-retrieved examples. Macro-F1 by frequency bin. GPT-5: 0.54 overall / head 0.68 / tail 0.53 / extreme tail 0.34. Best discriminative Llama-8B: 0.54 / 0.74 / 0.53 / 0.12. Generative Llama-70B: extreme tail 0.16. Also uncertainty quantification. No precision/recall split, no training-size sweep, no model combination. Data CC0 with splits on Hugging Face and code on GitHub.
works.bearing: Takes the core of claim 2 on the same data source: temporal split, frequency bins, retrieval-prompted LLM beating fine-tuned models only in the extreme tail, and fine-tuned LLMs (including 70B) not closing that gap. It leaves open our 1-5 bin, a training-size sweep, single-label leaf codes, natural-prevalence precision (its test is stratified and its rare labels are preserved by downsampling) and any per-report selector. It must be cited, and it supports our point that stratified tests overstate rare-code precision.

works.what_they_did: Zero- and few-shot ICD coding by tree search over the ontology, motivated by rare codes.

works.what_they_did: LoRA-tuned FLAN-T5 generative XBRL tagging; state of the art, attributed to zero-shot and least-frequent tags.
works.bearing: Counter-evidence to a general 'LoRA-tuned LLM does not close the tail gap' claim (its baseline is AttentionXML, not a prompted frontier LLM). The '35.3% macro-F1 gain on tags with fewer than 10 occurrences' is snippet-only.

works.bearing: Further evidence that LoRA-tuned decoders can help the tail. Frame our LoRA result as data-specific.

found.title: Has anyone measured LLM coders at natural prevalence?
found.answer:
Yes, people have measured LLM coders on natural, unbalanced streams. None that I found does what claim 3 does: count false rare-code answers per code, or pooled, for a zero-shot or retrieval-prompted LLM over hundreds of codes at about 1 in 1,000, and then show that a set of fixes fails.

The natural-stream studies I found split into three kinds:
(a) Random natural samples that are too small to say anything about rare codes. Rossow et al. 2025 coded 1,000 Zambian labour-force responses into 436 ISCO and 419 ISIC codes and state themselves that the sample cannot characterise rare categories. Feer et al. 2026 used 200 test narratives over 574 injury labels and report F1 only.
(b) Natural-frequency and later-period tests with fine-tuned, not zero-shot, generative models. Coutinho et al. 2026 coded Portuguese death certificates: 84k natural test items, 3,644 codes, plus a test on a later six months. Macro precision is about 21% at full-code level, against 80% accuracy. They tried conformal sets and probabilistic quantification but give no rare-code false-positive count.
(c) Binary or few-label tasks at real base rates. Liao et al. 2026 (ADR, 28 of 7,950, LLM after a rule trigger) count false positives, and a fix worked there: LoRA fine-tuning cut false positives from 16 to 7. Zhou et al. 2023 (NVDRS, 9 circumstances at 1.6-5%) report F1 only.

The second half of claim 3, that balanced or enriched tests overstate rare-class precision, is taken in principle by work outside LLM coding. Caswell et al. COLING 2020 is a many-class precedent: language ID over up to 1,629 languages, held-out balanced sets look fine, but human-judged web-crawl precision was about 5% for many low-resource languages. They say to report the false positive rate, and tunable wordlist filters plus semi-supervised models raised median precision from 5.5% to 71.2%. That result cuts against a general claim that "no fix works". A reviewer may ask why per-code keyword or wordlist filters with a precision knob were not tried. For LLMs specifically, the same point is made by a commentary using simulation (Chen 2026, rare-disease diagnosis) and by Norén et al. Drug Saf 2026; the first round already had Norén.

What stays open after this search:
- the measured per-code false-naming rate of zero-shot and retrieval LLMs across hundreds of codes at about 0.08% prevalence;
- scoring the same LLM systems under natural, stratified and balanced protocols on one coding task;
- the failure of a whole set of fixes at that prevalence (prior correction, prompt changes, memory filter, LLM agreement, encoder veto);
- the coverage ceiling (219 of 552 rare reports reached by any coder).

Confidence is medium, not high, because OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were unusable and Google Scholar and the statistical-office grey literature were not searched.

works.citation: Caswell I, Breiner T, van Esch D, Bapna A. Language ID in the Wild: Unexpected Challenges on the Path to a Thousand-Language Web Text Corpus. COLING 2020; arXiv 2010.14571
works.what_they_did: Language ID over up to 1,629 languages. Models that score well on held-out sets reach only about 5% human-judged precision on web crawl for many low-resource languages. Section 3.1 ('99% Accuracy Is Not Enough') gives the base-rate formula and says to report the false positive rate as well as precision measured on balanced data. Two fixes, tunable-precision wordlist filters and semi-supervised transformer LangID, raised median dataset precision from 5.5% to 71.2%.
works.bearing: Takes, in principle, 'balanced held-out tests overstate rare-class precision across hundreds of classes', in a non-LLM, non-coding task. It narrows claim 3's 'no fix works': there, per-class lexical filters with a precision knob did work. Our negative result has to be stated for zero-shot and retrieval LLM coders on report codes. A per-code keyword or wordlist filter is an untried fix that a reviewer could ask for.

works.citation: Coutinho I, Correia GM, Martins B, Moreira A, Peralta-Santos A. ICD coding of death certificates with generative language models. PLOS Digital Health 2026;5(2):e0001245
works.what_they_did: 843,103 Portuguese death certificates with 3,644 ICD-10 full codes and a long tail. Train/validation/test split 80/10/10 per code, so the test set has natural frequencies (84,292 items), plus a test on a later period (the last six months of 2021, 57,089 items). Models: fine-tuned BERTimbau and LLaMA-3.2 (fine-tuned or constrained decoding). Full-code accuracy about 80.6-81.1%, but macro precision only about 20-22%. On the later period, accuracy is 74.7% and macro precision 16.8%. They also tried conformal prediction sets and probabilistic classify-and-count quantification. False positives are plotted only for four specific causes. The 64 codes not seen in training were almost all missed.
works.bearing: The closest natural-stream, later-period, many-code study found. It takes 'evaluate code assignment at natural frequency on a later period, with quantification'. It leaves claim 3 alone: the models are fine-tuned, not zero-shot or retrieval-prompted; there is no per-code count of false rare-code answers; there is no fix-failure analysis. Its macro-vs-accuracy gap is consistent with our finding.

works.citation: Rossow T, Edison T, Hardie R, Mayne H. Transforming Zambia's Labour Force Survey using artificial intelligence. IGC Working Paper ZMB-25058, Oct 2025
works.what_they_did: A RAG plus few-shot LLM pipeline assigns 4-digit ISCO (436 choices) and ISIC (419 choices) codes to 1,000 Labour Force Survey responses. The responses are a random sample from the 2023 survey, labelled by experts at the Zambia Statistics Agency. Exact-match accuracy is 60-63% for ISCO and 57-66% for ISIC, 10-17 points above enumerators. The limitations section says the sample is too small to characterise accuracy on rare occupation and industry categories.
works.bearing: An LLM coding study on a natural random sample in official statistics, with a code list of several hundred. It does not count false rare-code answers and says it cannot. Leaves claim 3 open.

works.citation: Liao C, Lai X, Chen W, He J, Yu X. Trigger-first large language model-assisted adverse drug reaction surveillance: a pharmacist-supervised retrospective cohort study. Explor Res Clin Soc Pharm 2026; doi 10.1016/j.rcsop.2026.100866
works.what_they_did: 7,950 inpatient exposure episodes, 28 of them ADR-positive (about 0.35%). A rule trigger selected 167 candidates (2.1%) with 100% sensitivity. Qwen3-4B, base versus LoRA-fine-tuned, on the candidates: PPV 59% vs 79%. Fine-tuning cut false positives from 16 to 7.
works.bearing: An LLM at real pharmacovigilance base rates with false positives counted and a fix that worked. Binary, enriched by a trigger first, and with 28 positives. Narrows the general framing ('fixes fail at low prevalence') but not our many-code setting.

works.citation: Zhou W, Prater LC, Goldstein EV, Mooney SJ. Identifying Rare Circumstances Preceding Female Firearm Suicides: Validating a Large Language Model Approach. JMIR Ment Health 2023;10:e49359
works.what_they_did: 1,462 NVDRS narratives split 50/50 at natural frequencies. Nine circumstances, all under 5% prevalence (e.g. sleep problem 3.4%, sexual violence 2.6%, bullying 1.6%). Zero-shot FLAN-UL2 yes/no questions against SVMs. The LLM's F1 is above 0.6 for 4 circumstances and above 0.8 for 2. Bullying is near 0 for both.
works.bearing: An early precedent for 'zero-shot LLM beats a trained classifier on rare labels at natural prevalence' (claim 2 territory). Per-label binary questions at 1.6-5%, F1 only, no false-positive analysis. Leaves claim 3 alone.

works.citation: Feer et al. AI powered patient records analysis for injury surveillance in children and adolescents: a feasibility study from Switzerland. Int J Public Health 2026;71:1609472
works.what_they_did: 30,876 paediatric ED injury narratives. An adapted EU-IDB coding scheme cut from 1,187 to 574 labels. Mistral-7B fine-tuned with LoRA. Random 1,800/200 split. F1 only; level-3 macro F1 is 0.08-0.23. Bayesian classify-and-count for prevalence, with large prevalence gaps between predictions and annotations left unresolved.
works.bearing: A natural random test set with a large injury code list, but tiny and fine-tuned. No false rare-code counts. Leaves claim 3 open.

works.citation: Kähler M, Konermann K, Kluge L, Schumacher M. Does generative AI supersede supervised XMLC? A Benchmark Study on Automated Subject Indexing with German Scientific Literature. arXiv 2607.14882 (KONVENS 2026 submission)
works.what_they_did: German National Library subject indexing. The label space has 204,056 entities, and 8,978 distinct labels appear in a test set of 4,651 documents. Supervised XMLC is compared with three LLM methods. The test set is balanced across 20 subject groups, not natural. LLMs do better on propensity-weighted (tail-emphasising) scores and on graded relevance; XMLC does better on frequent labels. No false-positive rates for rare labels.
works.bearing: Another claim-2-type result (LLMs better on the tail), from extreme multi-label classification. Uses a balanced test design, so it never measures rare-label false naming at natural frequencies. Leaves claim 3 open.

works.citation: Chen I. Epidemiological spectrum bias limits the clinical validity of LLM-based rare disease diagnostics. Research Square preprint 2026, doi 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10042099/v1
works.what_they_did: A commentary arguing that LLM rare-disease benchmarks are artificially enriched and overstate real-world value. Monte Carlo simulations show PPV collapsing at realistic low prevalence.
works.bearing: Takes the argument that enriched or stratified benchmarks overstate LLM rare-class precision, for LLMs, by simulation only. The empirical comparison of the same coders under natural, stratified and balanced protocols stays open.

works.citation: Perron BE, Stoll D, Victor BG, Qia Z, Jud A, Ryan JP. Validation of a Small Language Model for DSM-5 Substance Category Classification in Child Welfare Records. arXiv 2603.06836 (2026)
works.what_they_did: A local 20B LLM sorts substance mentions in child-maltreatment narratives into 7 DSM-5 categories. Validated on 900 stratified cases. Five common categories reach kappa 0.94-1.00 and precision 92-100%. The two low-prevalence categories (hallucinogen, inhalant) performed poorly.
works.bearing: A small, stratified example of LLM weakness on rare categories. Not natural prevalence, no per-code false-positive rate. Leaves claim 3 alone.

works.citation: INSEE SSP Hub project: Recoding NACE 2.0 to NACE 2.1 with LLMs (2026)
works.what_they_did: About 1.4M multivocal business-activity records recoded into NACE 2.1 (732 categories). The LLM chooses only among the correspondence-table candidates (RBAG), with a 3-model majority vote. Accuracy is 78% on about 30,000 expert-annotated records, and about 10 points better than plain RAG. A classifier retrained on the LLM labels reaches about 80%.
works.bearing: Large-scale LLM coding in official statistics with candidate restriction. Restricting candidates is a known way to stop free naming of codes. No per-code or rare-code false positives are reported. Leaves claim 3 open.

works.citation: Gershon A, Soffer S, Nadkarni GN, Klang E. Automatic ICD coding using LLMs: a systematic review. medRxiv 2025, doi 10.1101/2025.07.30.25330916
works.what_they_did: A PROSPERO-registered review of 35 studies. Median micro-F1 on frequent codes is 0.79; median macro-F1 on infrequent codes is 0.42. Only 3 studies did external validation.
works.bearing: No reviewed study is described as measuring rare-code false positives at natural prevalence. Supports the view that this gap exists in clinical ICD coding, though from the abstract only.

works.citation: Gan Y, Rybinski M, Hachey B, Kummerfeld JK. Aligning AI Research with the Needs of Clinical Coding Workflows: Eight Recommendations Based on US Data Analysis and Critical Review. ACL 2025, doi 10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.45
works.what_they_did: Criticises evaluation on the MIMIC top-50 code set as an oversimplification when thousands of codes are used in practice, and gives eight recommendations for evaluation.
works.bearing: Part of the evaluation-critique literature that Eng 2026 cites for stratified sampling. The abstract does not mention natural-prevalence false positives, so it does not take claim 3. The eight recommendations were not read.

works.citation: Achananuparp P, Lim E-P, Lu Y. A Multi-Stage Framework with Taxonomy-Guided Reasoning for Occupation Classification Using Large Language Models. arXiv 2503.12989 (ICWSM 2026)
works.what_they_did: Inference, retrieval and reranking stages for occupation (and skill) classification against a taxonomy, compared with GPT-4o.
works.bearing: The abstract gives no rare-occupation or natural-prevalence analysis. Leaves claim 3 alone.

works.citation: Muaz, Janjua, Loughran, St John Lynch. A Framework for LLM-Guided and ISO 5338-Aligned Data Engineering in Medical Device Adverse Event Reporting. IFIP AIAI 2026, doi 10.1007/978-3-032-30805-4_1
works.what_they_did: According to a search snippet, GPT-OSS-120B coding MAUDE reports into IMDRF device-problem codes reaches 59.49% 'consensus' at level 1 and 23.04% at a deeper level. The authors argue that zero-shot prompting is not enough.
works.bearing: An LLM coding MAUDE with IMDRF codes, on the same dataset as ours, and it should be cited. Its numbers are unverified (the publisher and university pages refused access), and nothing suggests a natural-prevalence rare-code analysis.

now_taken: Balanced or held-out test sets overstate rare-class precision over hundreds of classes, with the base-rate formula and advice to report the false positive rate: Caswell et al. COLING 2020 (language ID, up to 1,629 classes, about 5% crawl precision for many low-resource languages; full text read). Also, for LLMs, by simulation: Chen 2026 commentary. The general argument cannot be claimed; only an empirical same-system comparison under natural, stratified and balanced protocols on a coding task can.

Per-class fixes can rescue rare-class precision at web scale (Caswell 2020: 5.5% to 71.2% median precision with tunable wordlist filters and semi-supervised models). At real pharmacovigilance base rates, a trigger plus LoRA fine-tuning cut LLM false positives (Liao 2026). The negative result 'no fix works' must be stated narrowly: zero-shot and retrieval-prompted LLM coders over a code list, and the specific fixes we tried.

Evaluating a generative coder on a natural-frequency test set plus a test on a later period, over thousands of codes, with conformal sets and classify-and-count quantification: Coutinho et al. PLOS Digit Health 2026 (fine-tuned LLaMA on death certificates; macro precision about 21% against 80% accuracy).

LLM coding into several hundred official-statistics codes on a natural random sample: Rossow et al. IGC 2025 (436 ISCO and 419 ISIC codes, n=1,000), INSEE NACE 2.1 recoding (732 codes; candidate-restricted LLM vote).
Zero-shot LLM beats a trained classifier on rare labels at natural prevalence: Zhou et al. JMIR Ment Health 2023 (NVDRS, 1.6-5%). This is another precedent for claim 2.
still_open: A measured per-code (and pooled) false-naming rate of zero-shot and retrieval-prompted LLM coders across hundreds of codes in a natural stream at about 1 in 1,000 (our 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports, 97% of rare answers false). Searched in occupation/industry coding (ISCO, SOC, NACE), OIICS and NEISS injury coding, cause-of-death ICD-10, MedDRA and pharmacovigilance, cancer registries and ICD-O, clinical ICD coding, XMLC subject indexing, incident reports and content moderation: about 32 API queries plus 10 web searches and citation chasing from Norén, Martin and Zhou. Every LLM study found is small and random (n=200-1,000), stratified or balanced, binary at 0.35% or more, or fine-tuned rather than zero-shot.

A set of fixes tested on held-out years and failing at that prevalence: prior correction, prompt changes, memory filter, LLM agreement and encoder veto. The only fixes found in natural-prevalence studies (Caswell wordlists, Liao LoRA, Coutinho conformal and quantification) are either successes in other settings or are not scored on rare-code precision. Not contradicted, but per-code wordlist or keyword filters with a precision knob are untried and a reviewer may ask for them.

An empirical, same-system comparison of natural, stratified and balanced test protocols on an LLM coding task, showing by how much the latter overstate rare-code precision. Only arguments and simulations were found (Caswell 2020, Chen 2026, Norén 2026).
The coverage ceiling: the share of rare-code reports that any of several coders reaches (219 of 552). Nothing comparable was found, though I did not search for it specifically.

How hard I looked: medium. OpenAlex (including cites: citation chasing) was entirely unavailable, Semantic Scholar was mostly unavailable, and Google Scholar, ACL Anthology full-text search and the statistical-office grey literature (AIML4OS WP10, UNECE HLG-MOS, ONS ClassifAI) were not searched or read.

found.title: The unread 2026 venue papers and the citing neighbourhood
found.answer:
This round adds a little to the first one and takes none of our three claims outright. Search tools were the main limit. OpenAlex hit its daily limit for this network after about 6 calls, and the error said it resets at midnight UTC. Semantic Scholar returned 429 errors on most calls. The arXiv API returned empty or wrong results. ScienceDirect, PolyU and CityU pages refused access (403). So the planned OpenAlex citation chase did not happen.

1. The five venue papers. ESWA 131366 (Villanueva-García et al.) is not relevant: it tests 4,109 pipelines on one binary task, retirement detection in Spanish social-security records, with 2.34% positives. EAAI 114798 (Smetana, Salles de Salles & Khazanovich) uses GPT-3.5 with zero- and few-shot prompts plus ML clustering on OSHA highway work-zone narratives. Its abstract shows no fine-tuned coder alongside the LLM, no rare-class analysis and no temporal split.
   - For Ding EAAI 115750, Hou EAAI 114403 and Chhetri AEI 105391, no abstract could be reached in OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, ScienceDirect or 3 web searches. For Ding, the nearest evidence is Yi Ding's 2025 CityU thesis (supervisor Min Xie). There an LLM writes synthetic descriptions for minority failure modes, and a BERT prompt-tuning hierarchical classifier is trained on them. So the LLM adds training data; it is not a second coder. This is inferred and not confirmed for the EAAI article.
   - Hou's title points to a classic selective ensemble on imbalanced civil-aviation maintenance hazard text. Chhetri's title points to a small-language-model benchmark on incident narratives. Neither is confirmed.
2. Citation chase. Semantic Scholar and Europe PMC both give EnergyRoute 0 citing works. Semantic Scholar gives Martin et al. 0. Stewart, Hodkiewicz & Li has 20 citers, and none routes or selects between coders. Citers of Emer and MADE could not be fetched.
3. The most useful new find is Li, Tang, Xia et al. (arXiv 2512.21041, LAK26). In their human-AI workflow, an item goes to human experts when MacBERT's confidence is below 0.6 or when the code it proposed is rare (under 5% of the data). That is the frequency of the proposed code, used after the answer, to route an item. It is a fixed rule that sends items to people over 12 codes, not a learned selector among three coders. Still, the paper must not say that idea is unused.
   - The same paper partly cuts against claim 2. With 12 dialogue codes, zero-shot GPT-4o did not beat fine-tuned BERT on rare codes: kappa was near zero for both on most of them.
4. Li H, He, …, Feng (npj Digit Med 2026, full text) had an LLM assign MAUDE device-problem codes from the 487 IMDRF codes. Human judges preferred the LLM's code to the filer's in 60.8 of 90 reports and the filer's in 21.7, with ties in the rest. This settles the critic's open evidence question. It also supports our label-noise caveat for claim 3: some 'false' rare-code answers may be correct.
5. Soria's CatLLM (SocArXiv 2026, abstract only) finds that every one of 21 LLMs over-labels open survey answers, with precision 40 to 50 points below sensitivity. It reports unanimous multi-model ensembles and an 'Other' category as fixes. This narrows claim 3: the over-naming is published in a general form. Our result that agreement does not fix it at 1 in 1,000 is now set against a report that unanimity helps at much higher prevalence.
6. No 2026 work on coding FAA service difficulty report (SDR) PartCondition fields, or on assigning MAUDE device-problem codes over hundreds of leaf codes with a fine-tuned coder alongside an LLM, turned up beyond Li H and MADE, both already known.

works.citation: Ding Y, Zhu F, Li H, Xie M (2026). A large language model-augmented hierarchical text classification approach for intelligent failure data management. Eng Appl Artif Intell 115750 (Oct 2026).
works.what_they_did: Metadata only (OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar: no abstract; ScienceDirect 403). Inferred from Yi Ding's CityU thesis abstract (https://scholars.cityu.edu.hk/en/studentTheses/unlocking-maintenance-knowledge-an-industrial-knowledge-graph-ena/, read): wind-farm failure records from mainland China; a BERT-based hierarchy-aware prompt-tuning classifier for few-shot settings; an LLM prompt module generates synthetic failure descriptions for minority failure modes in the label hierarchy. Label source, number of classes and split not stated.

Cite as a venue neighbour on LLM help for rare failure modes. Unconfirmed until the article is read.

works.citation: Li Z, Tang L, Xia M, Li X, Chen N, Gasevic D, Fan Y (2025). When LLMs fall short in deductive coding: model comparison and human-AI collaboration workflow design. arXiv 2512.21041 (LAK26).
works.what_they_did: Medical-dialogue coding (77,420 turns, 12 codes, coded by two medical experts; tail = codes under 5%) and a 14-code English set. Fine-tuned BERT/RoBERTa/MacBERT against zero-shot Qwen3, DeepSeek-V3.1 and GPT-4o. Rare-code kappa was near zero for both families; the optimised MacBERT reached 0.18-0.36 on some rare codes. In the workflow, an item goes to human experts if MacBERT's confidence is under 0.6 or the predicted code is rare (under 5%); this flagged 44 of 500 items and raised kappa from 0.62 to 0.66.
works.bearing: Narrows claim 1: it routes on the frequency of the code the classifier proposed, after the answer, as a fixed rule that sends items to people. Our learned selector across three coders with a frozen later year is still different, but the signal must not be called unused. Weakly against claim 2 at a very different scale (12 codes): LLMs did not beat BERT on rare codes. Does not touch claim 3 (no natural-proportion precision).

works.citation: Li H, He X, Subbaswamy A, Vossler P, Gossmann A, Singh K, Feng J (2026). Scaling medical device regulatory science using large language models. NPJ Digit Med 9:221.
works.what_they_did: An LLM pipeline over 1,841 MAUDE reports for AI/ML devices assigns the event type and device product problem code (the most detailed of 487 IMDRF codes). Against the filer's code, human judges preferred the LLM's problem code in 60.8 of 90 reports and the filer's in 21.7, with 7.5 ties (Table 2); GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 as judges gave about 80% LLM wins.
works.bearing: Already known to the project. It now gives a sourced figure that MAUDE filer problem codes are often judged worse than an LLM's, which supports our label-noise caveat for claim 3 (some 'false' rare answers may be right). There is no fine-tuned encoder, no rare-code analysis and no temporal split, so claims 1 and 2 are untouched.

Fixes adopted: verbose definitions with include/exclude rules, unanimous multi-model ensembles, an automatic 'Other' category.
works.bearing: Narrows claim 3: LLM over-naming that inflates category prevalence is published in a general form. It reports unanimity and definitions as fixes, so our statement that LLM agreement and prompt changes do not fix it must be scoped to rare codes at about 1 in 1,000 over hundreds of codes. Category counts and prevalences are not in the abstract.

works.what_they_did: Long-tailed, hierarchical multi-label medical device adverse-event benchmark with strict time-based splits; more than 20 encoder and decoder models, fine-tuned and few-shot. found.title: Regulator-coded report streams outside the US, and the candidates left unchecked
found.answer:
None of the non-US regulator streams I could check meets our needs. Each fails on public text, on who chooses the code, or on access:
- Korea's MFDS publishes on data.go.kr only its adverse-event code list, a table of follow-up actions (flags and dates, no text) and recall reports.
- Korea's consumer-injury file (KCA CISS) has 23,192 rows, all coded fields, with no narrative column.
- Korean rail data (978 rows for 2021-2025) and aviation data (statistics and taxonomies only) have no report text.
- Health Canada's medical device incident data carry per-incident IMDRF codes but have no narrative field.
- Australia's TGA DAEN has public event descriptions, but a 2026 paper says these are not coded in standard terminology, and nearly all reports come from industry.
- Japan's PMDA publishes line lists; detailed records come only on disclosure request.
- EUDAMED's vigilance module is not mandatory before 2027 or 2028, and whether the public will see it is not settled.

Of the candidates the first round dropped, VAERS is real but weak for us: the narrative is up to 32,000 characters and MedDRA terms are derived from it, but the terms are listed alphabetically with no principal term, the guide does not say who the coders are, and the bulk download asks for a verification code. LLM-based MedDRA coding of VAERS text is already published (He et al. 2025, abstract read). The NIOSH OIICS competition set has only 48 codes and no dates. MSHA has a 384-character narrative and several coded fields, but I could not confirm who assigns the codes or how many each field has. The full ATSB occurrence export is restricted, and dashboard exports stop at 200 rows. NEISS stays the best new candidate. CPSC's NEISS query page now lists archived annual data for 2025, so a 2023/2024/2025 split is possible. No terms of use appear anywhere.

Two corrections to the first round:
- The first round's critic was wrong: a 27 May 2025 blog post (Circo, full text read) did have gpt-4o-mini with retrieval pick NEISS product codes for 500 narratives from 2024, at 66.40% accuracy, counting a match to any of Product_1-3. So LLM product-code assignment on NEISS is no longer untouched, though only informally.
- Two works narrow our selector and ranked-list claims without taking them. Marucci-Wellman et al. 2017 (abstract read) send narratives to manual review either by prediction strength or by agreement between classifiers, and pass rare or ambiguous cases to people. The BLS autocoder (page read) assigns survey injury codes only above a confidence threshold, about 81-92% of codes in 2021-2023.

I found no study of NEISS, VAERS, MSHA or any non-US device stream that does what we do: a training-support selector, rare-versus-frequent results by frequency band, or rare-code precision at natural proportions.

works.citation: Signal detection of adverse events in medical devices using natural language processing: a case study in pelvic mesh. Sci Rep 2026, doi 10.1038/s41598-026-50950-z (PMC13319759)
works.what_they_did: Topic modelling of free-text TGA DAEN device reports from 2012-2017 (14,170 reports), followed by disproportionality signal detection. Two clinicians reviewed reports to measure misclassification.
works.bearing: Establishes DAEN facts: event descriptions are public, and device reports are 'not coded using standard medical terminology'. That rules DAEN out as a code-labelled stream. It takes none of our claims.

works.citation: Failure modes of robotic-assisted arthroplasty platforms in Australia: a descriptive analysis of TGA adverse event reports. J Robot Surg 2026, doi 10.1007/s11701-026-03890-9 (PMC13541923)
works.what_they_did: Searched DAEN for July 2012 to December 2025 and used the 'Event Type' failure-mode field plus the 'Event Description' narrative. Of 140 reports, 97.9% were submitted by industry, and the authors note that failure-mode coding may vary between sponsors.
works.bearing: Confirms that the DAEN code is chosen by the sponsor, the same weakness as MAUDE. It does not touch our claims.

works.citation: Signal Detection Using Change Point Analysis to Identify Safety Signals from Spontaneous Reports in Aortic Stent Grafts in Japan. J Med Syst 2026, doi 10.1007/s10916-026-02388-z (PMC13106239)
works.what_they_did: Analysed 20,678 PMDA malfunction and adverse-event reports on aortic stent grafts (2008-2022). The researchers mapped them to the JFMDA problem terminology themselves. The data came through an AMED project and are not public; PMDA disclosure requests are the only route.
works.bearing: Shows that detailed PMDA records are not openly downloadable, which rules out PMDA as a public dataset. It does not touch our claims.

works.citation: Circo G. Fine Tuning Your LLM for Fun and Profit, Part I (blog), 27 May 2025
works.what_they_did: Had gpt-4o-mini pick NEISS product codes for 500 narratives from 2024. An all-mpnet retriever first narrowed the list of more than 800 products. Accuracy was 66.40%, counting a match to any of Product_1-3, and the post also reports accuracy for the products the LLM named most often.
works.bearing: Takes 'nobody has had an LLM assign NEISS product codes'. This is informal, not peer-reviewed, a single coder on a small sample, with no frequency bins, selector, temporal test or natural-prevalence analysis. It corrects the first-round critic, who said the post was about injury or body part.

works.citation: Marucci-Wellman HR, Corns HL, Lehto MR. Classifying injury narratives of large administrative databases for surveillance: a practical approach combining machine learning ensembles and human review. Accid Anal Prev 2017, doi 10.1016/j.aap.2016.10.014
works.what_they_did: Coded workers' compensation narratives into BLS OIICS event codes with NB, SVM and LR. They compared filtering to manual review by prediction strength against filtering by agreement between algorithms. Sending the weakest 30% of LR predictions to people gave 0.89 sensitivity/PPV; a triple ensemble reached 0.93 with 41% left for manual review. Rare, emerging or ambiguous narratives were explicitly routed to people.
works.bearing: Narrows Claim 1 and Claim 3. Per-report routing between machine and people, by confidence or by classifier agreement, and a manual queue for rare cases are established practice in injury coding. It does not take a selector that uses each proposed code's training support, an LLM-versus-encoder split, or natural-prevalence precision.

works.citation: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Automated coding of SOII case narratives (web page)

It moved from logistic regression (2014-17) to neural networks and then a transformer from 2021. A code is assigned only above a confidence threshold: about 85% of codes in 2019, 92% in 2021-22, and 81% in 2023.
works.bearing: Shows that a confidence cascade to human coders is the operational standard at a statistical agency. That supports comparing against a confidence cascade (Claim 1) without taking the selector. Narratives are not public.

works.citation: Bertke SJ et al. Comparison of methods for auto-coding causation of injury narratives. Accid Anal Prev 2016, doi 10.1016/j.aap.2015.12.006
works.what_they_did: Compared naive Bayes with logistic models for OIICS event coding of workers' compensation narratives, and tested on BLS narratives.
works.bearing: Background on autocoding injury narratives. It leaves our claims alone.

found.title: Ranked read-first lists at very low prevalence over many categories
found.answer:
After a second, fuller search, the ranked read-first list still cannot be claimed as a method. It is a two-phase TAR workflow: a ranker trained once, frozen, and then read in order. Every piece of it has a precedent somewhere. What is still unpublished is the operating point, and the paper should make that its claim. The operating point is hundreds of rare codes pooled into one queue, positives at about 0.08%, a ranker frozen on one year and checked on later years, LLM proposals and encoder scores as the ranking features, and a reader who must also name the code.

Known since the first round (in result.json): TAR's measures and stopping rules, LLM plus ranker (Bron 2024), a frozen classifier used on a live stream (Cochrane RCT Classifier), and regulator triage of safety reports.

New this round:
- TAR experiments do go down to rare single categories, but they stop above us. In the full text of Yang, Lewis & Frieder's heuristic stopping-rules paper (DocEng 2021), the 'Rare' bin includes an RCV1 category at prevalence 0.002133, and the lowest prevalence bin was not used.
- The same paper says a sample-based recall check needs about 385 positives, which is about 38,500 documents at 1% prevalence. By my own arithmetic (not from any source), that is roughly 480,000 reads at 0.08%. So recall cannot be certified by random sampling at our prevalence. A reviewer will ask what the paper does instead.
- Real e-discovery does handle many categories with a reader who assigns the category. In the Irish case reported at CEUR Vol-3832 (Harbison, Grossman, Cormack et al.; full text), 70 requests for production were grouped into 10 composite categories. Each category got its own active-learning review (CAL), followed by a sub-review to assign the specific request. The authors report that sorting documents into categories was of very limited value, but the details are in a 2024 paper I could not open.
- Rare-class search over many classes at once also exists: multiclass active search with diversity (Nguyen & Garnett, full text: images, a citation network and drug discovery, with hit rates around 2-36%), and exemplar-guided active learning with a stopping rule per rare class (Hartford et al., NeurIPS 2020: word senses, using language-model embeddings).
- On removing the human: the full text of Available Guardrails (arXiv 2609.22048) gives the cost of certifying precision per unit. At target precision 0.90 and true error 0.05, one group needs 179 served calibration examples for 80% availability, fifty groups need 450 each, and the floor is 29 selected examples. Codes with 1-5 reports cannot meet that.
- Other routes to automatic acceptance guarantee only an average over all labels or cover something else. Conformal Labeling (Huang et al., NeurIPS 2026) controls the overall false-labelling rate. Long-tail conformal prediction (Ding, Fermanian & Salmon) is about prediction-set coverage, not precision. Conformal selection (Jin & Candès, JMLR) controls the false-discovery rate of a shortlist.
- The nearest low-prevalence LLM triage I found is binary: Liao et al. 2026, 28 positives in 7,950 (0.35%), trigger first and then an LLM. The authors say the LLM must not be used as an autonomous exclusion rule.

I found no published case of automatic acceptance working at about 1 in 1,000 across many rare classes.

What a TAR or IR reviewer would accept as new: the pooled multi-code operating point at 0.08%, the year-to-year freeze on safety and failure report streams, and the measured failure of automatic acceptance there. They would not accept the ranked list itself as new.

Baselines and measures they would ask for:
- Baselines: random order; encoder-only ranking; LLM-only ranking; a per-code TF-IDF logistic two-phase TAR baseline; simulated CAL/AutoTAR (BMI), per code and pooled; Bron-style LLM-then-CAL.
- Measures: gain curves, recall at k reads, reads needed to reach recall r, WSS@r, the spread of recall across codes, and how many distinct codes are found (diversity, as in multiclass active search).
- Stopping and certification: a stopping rule with a recall estimate (QuantCI, Chao's estimator, Delayed Countdown), or an explicit statement that certification is infeasible at this prevalence; and a test of pooled conformal selection or Conformal Labeling as the published automation route.
- Code naming: a separate measure of how accurately the reader names the code, ideally with agreement between readers.

works.citation: Yang E, Lewis DD, Frieder O. Heuristic Stopping Rules for Technology-Assisted Review. DocEng 2021. arXiv 2106.09871
works.what_they_did: Compared target-aware heuristic stopping rules (Quant, QuantCI, BatchPos, Knee) with sample-based rules on RCV1-v2 (804,414 docs, 658 categories), choosing 5 categories from each of 9 prevalence-by-difficulty bins. The lowest and highest prevalence bins were not used. Their worked example is the Rare-Medium category I24000 at prevalence 0.002133. They note that a recall estimate within 0.05 at 95% confidence needs about 385 relevant documents in a random sample, about 38,500 documents at 1% prevalence.
works.bearing: Narrows the TAR-at-low-prevalence item. Single-category TAR has been run down to about 0.2%, but the rarest band is left out on purpose, so the 0.08% pooled band is still unstudied. It also implies that sample-based certification of our list is infeasible: by my own arithmetic, about 480,000 reads at 0.08%.

works.citation: Harbison A, Grossman MR, Cormack GV, McManus B, O'Halloran T. Factors Affecting the Performance of Reviewers in a Large-Scale Technology-Assisted Review Project. CEUR-WS Vol-3832 (2024), paper 1
works.what_they_did: A real Irish litigation review of more than 300 million documents. The 70 requests for production were too many to review at once, so they were grouped into 10 composite categories. Each was reviewed with CAL on two platforms, followed by a sub-review that assigned each responsive document to its specific request. Reviewer disagreement made recall estimates unreliable, and elusion testing was highly unreliable. The authors also report that sorting documents into categories was of very limited value; that finding is in their ICIM 2024 paper, which I did not open.
works.bearing: Takes the idea that many-category review with the reader assigning the category is new in practice. Its design is grouping plus a separate CAL per group, not one pooled frozen ranking. Prevalence per category is not reported. Our pooled 0.08% queue with code naming is still not covered, but we should cite it, along with the warning about reader disagreement on category assignment.

works.citation: Priye P, Wang Y, Ling H, Chaykowsky M. Available Guardrails: Certifying Selective Prediction across ML Systems. arXiv 2609.22048 (Sep 2026)
works.what_they_did: Certifies the precision of a selective predictor per reporting unit by exact-binomial inversion. Worked costs: at target precision 0.90, failure probability 0.05 and true selective error 0.05, one group needs 179 served calibration examples for 80% availability, and fifty groups need 450 each. In an appendix example, certification needs at least 29 selected examples.
works.bearing: Takes 'automatic acceptance per rare code with a precision guarantee is impossible' as a general result. Our codes with 1-5 reports cannot reach these counts, so our negative result follows from known arithmetic. We should cite it rather than present the result as a discovery.

works.citation: Nguyen Q, Garnett R. Nonmyopic Multiclass Active Search with Diminishing Returns for Diverse Discovery. arXiv 2202.03593 (preprint)
works.what_they_did: Active search over several rare target classes, with a diminishing-returns utility that rewards finding members of many different classes. Tested on Fashion-MNIST (about 2% target rate), Photoswitch, CiteSeerX (about 14% hit rate) and drug discovery.
works.bearing: Already states our objective (finds per read across many rare classes, with diversity). It uses Bayesian models updated during the search, no text LLMs, and prevalences far above 0.08%. A reviewer may ask for a per-code diversity measure, such as how many distinct codes are found within k reads.

works.citation: Hartford J, Leyton-Brown K, Raviv H, Padnos D, Lev S, Lenz B. Exemplar Guided Active Learning. NeurIPS 2020. arXiv 2011.01285
works.what_they_did: Searches language-model embedding space for rare classes (word senses) under a labelling budget. A stopping rule drops a class once it is shown, with high probability, to fall below a frequency threshold. Cost is proven to be within a log factor of an oracle.
works.bearing: Already does multi-class rare discovery with LM embeddings and a stopping rule per class. Its goal is a classifier above a frequency threshold, not recall of every rare item in a stream, and it has no LLM proposals and no time split.

works.citation: Huang H, Liao W, Xi H, Zeng H, Zhao M, Wei H. Provable Selective Auto-labeling with Reliability Guarantees (Conformal Labeling). NeurIPS 2026 poster
works.what_they_did: Selects which auto-generated labels (including LLM outputs) to accept, with finite-sample control of the false-labelling rate, using conformal p-values and Benjamini-Hochberg. The remaining labels go to people.
works.bearing: A published, tested route for automatic acceptance of LLM labels. Its guarantee is an average over all labels, which frequent codes dominate. It says nothing per rare code, and the poster page does not mention rare classes. Not shown to work at 1 in 1,000. A reviewer could ask us to run it, pooled over rare-code proposals.

works.citation: Jin Y, Candès EJ. Selection by Prediction with Conformal p-values. JMLR 2023. arXiv 2210.01408
works.what_they_did: Wraps any predictor to shortlist candidates whose unobserved outcome is likely positive, with false-discovery-rate control, using conformal p-values and BH. Applied to hiring and drug discovery.
works.bearing: The likeliest untried automation baseline: an FDR-controlled shortlist of pooled rare-code proposals. The abstract gives no class balance, and I found no application at about 0.08%. Still open whether it has any power there.

works.citation: Ding T, Fermanian J-B, Salmon J. Conformal Prediction for Long-Tailed Classification. arXiv 2507.06867 (v3 Feb 2026)
works.what_they_did: A prevalence-adjusted softmax score, plus interpolation between marginal and class-conditional thresholds, to trade prediction-set size against class-conditional coverage on Pl@ntNet-300K (1,081 classes) and iNaturalist-2018 (8,142 classes).
works.bearing: Narrows: this is long-tail conformal work over thousands of classes, but about coverage of prediction sets, not the precision of a single accepted label. It does not answer automatic acceptance.

works.citation: Liao C, Lai X, Chen W, He J, Yu X. Trigger-first large language model-assisted adverse drug reaction surveillance: a pharmacist-supervised retrospective cohort study. Explor Res Clin Soc Pharm 2026, doi 10.1016/j.rcsop.2026.100866
works.what_they_did: 7,950 inpatient episodes, 28 ADR-positive (about 0.35%). A rule trigger selected 167 candidates (2.10%) with 100% sensitivity. Qwen3-4B base versus LoRA-tuned then reviewed them: PPV 58.97% versus 78.79%, sensitivity 82.14% versus 92.86%. The authors conclude the LLM should support pharmacist review and not serve as an autonomous exclusion rule.
works.bearing: Takes 'a cheap first stage then LLM review at low prevalence keeps the human' for a single binary event. It does not cover many codes or 0.08%.

works.citation: Li H, He X, Subbaswamy A, Vossler P, Gossmann A, Singh K, Feng J. Scaling medical device regulatory science using large language models. NPJ Digit Med 2026, doi 10.1038/s41746-026-02353-7
works.what_they_did: Validates LLM extraction from FDA documents. One application codes medical device reports (1,841 MDRs for AI/ML-enabled devices) with the lowest-level codes from 487 IMDRF device problem codes. It notes that assigned codes vary with the coder's view and are poorly standardised.
works.bearing: Not about ranking. It is close to the project as a whole (LLM coding of MAUDE device problem codes, with FDA-affiliated authors) and should be cited. It produces no read-first list and no rare-code analysis at natural proportions.

works.citation: Ball R, Talal AH, Dang O, Muñoz M, Markatou M. Trust but Verify: Lessons Learned for the Application of AI to Case-Based Clinical Decision-Making From Postmarketing Drug Safety Assessment at the US FDA. J Med Internet Res 2024, doi 10.2196/50274
works.what_they_did: An FDA viewpoint on why some AI tools for case-report assessment were accepted by safety reviewers and others were not. Trust was the deciding factor, and the reviewers' decision process is poorly defined.
works.bearing: Leaves our claims alone. It supports framing the list as an aid that keeps the human, and confirms that regulators have worked on rare-event identification in case reports.

works.citation: Lewis DD, Emory T, Gray L, Noel M, Pickens J, Yang E. The Delayed Countdown Method for Validating Review-Oriented AI Workflows in eDiscovery. arXiv 2610.31311 (Oct 2026)
works.what_they_did: A validation method that can be added to existing review workflows, works with any stopping rule, and gives frequentist confidence intervals on effectiveness.
works.bearing: The current baseline for 'when can people stop reading'. The abstract does not mention low prevalence or multiple categories, so how it behaves at 0.08% pooled is open and measurable.

works.citation: Fletcher A, Stevenson M. Confidence-Based Stopping Methods for Systematic Reviews. arXiv 2606.15380 (Jun 2026)
works.what_they_did: Two heuristic stopping methods that check whether the documents screened so far support the review's conclusion rather than a recall target. Tested on a Diagnostic Test Accuracy collection.
works.bearing: Leaves our claims alone. It is a 2026 stopping-rule alternative a reviewer might name; there is no low-prevalence or multi-category test.

now_taken: Two-phase TAR (rank once, freeze, read in order) and its stopping rules as the framework for our list. The list itself is not a method contribution.
TAR on single categories down to about 0.2% prevalence (RCV1 'Rare' bin, e.g. I24000 at 0.002133), with the lowest prevalence bin deliberately excluded. Only the band below this is unstudied.

Many-category e-discovery where the reader also assigns the category (70 requests grouped into 10 categories, separate CAL per group, then sub-review to the specific request; Harbison et al., CEUR 2024). This exists in practice, but not as one pooled frozen ranking and with no prevalence reported.

The objective of finding as many rare-class items per read across several classes, with diversity (multiclass active search), and LM-embedding search for many rare classes with a per-class stopping rule (Exemplar Guided Active Learning, NeurIPS 2020).

Certifying precision per rare unit needs tens to hundreds of calibration examples per unit (Available Guardrails: 179 for one group, 450 each for fifty, at least 29). Our 'no rule can auto-accept rare codes' is a known consequence and should be cited as one.
Overall-average guarantees for automatic acceptance of LLM labels (Conformal Labeling, NeurIPS 2026; conformal selection, Jin & Candès). These are published but do not give per-code precision.
LLM review behind a cheap first stage at 0.35% prevalence for one binary event, with authors rejecting autonomous use (Liao 2026).
LLM coding of MAUDE device-problem codes from the 487 IMDRF codes by an FDA-affiliated group (Li H et al., npj Digit Med 2026). This is relevant to the whole paper, not just the list.
still_open: Recall against reads for one pooled ranking over hundreds of rare codes at about 0.08% combined prevalence, where the reader must also name the code. taken: Claim 2 (LLMs win on rare codes, the encoder wins on frequent ones), on our own data source. MADE (Agarwal et al., ACL 2026, arXiv 2604.15203) uses openFDA device reports, 1,154 IMDRF labels, a strict temporal split (train 2015-2023, test Jul 2024-Jun 2025), macro-F1 by training-frequency bin, and a GPT-5 prompted with 10 kNN-retrieved examples (our retrieval coder). GPT-5 is about 0.34 on the extreme tail against about 0.16 for the best fine-tuned model, ties on the tail and loses on the head. Fine-tuned Llama up to 70B (LoRA and full) does not close the gap. I re-opened the html. Also shown in other domains: Motzfeldt 2025, Yock/Eng 2026, Martin/Feng/Peng ICHI 2026, Emer 2026, Zhou JMIR MH 2023, Kaehler 2026 (XMLC). Claim 2 is a replication, except for the per-bin training-size sweep.

An encoder, a kNN/retrieval tier and an LLM routed over about 300 imbalanced classes, reported by head/mid/tail group, with a later-year test, beating the encoder (+0.04 macro-F1) and a FrugalGPT confidence cascade: EnergyRoute (Jang et al., Sci Rep 2026). I re-opened the full text. Train 2018-2020; test 500 stratified items from 2021; thresholds are percentiles of the energy of the incoming test batch.

Using how rare the proposed code is as a routing trigger, after the classifier answers: Li Z et al. arXiv 2512.21041 (LAK26). I re-opened the html. MacBERT's answer goes to an expert, with GPT-4o adjudication, when confidence is below 0.6 or the predicted code occurs in under 5% of samples; this flagged 44 of 500 items and kappa went from 0.62 to 0.66. STREAQ (EMNLP Industry 2025) sends the small model's rare 'answer of interest' to a large LLM, in a binary setting. Judging a classifier by the class it outputs: Local Class Accuracy / BKS. So claim 1 cannot say the support of the proposed code is an unused signal.

A learned per-item deferral between an encoder and an LLM (logistic model over confidence features), and stacking or deferral over several experts plus an LLM: L2D-Clinical arXiv 2604.13285, AspectBench Front AI 2026, Arora et al. EMNLP Industry 2024, CMBS, Emer 2026. Confidence cascades are a published method and run in production (BLS autocoder; Marucci-Wellman 2017 routes by prediction strength or by classifier agreement and sends rare narratives to people).

Balanced or held-out tests overstate rare-class precision over hundreds of classes. Stated with the base-rate formula and the advice to report the false positive rate: Caswell et al. COLING 2020 (language ID). For LLMs, by simulation: Chen 2026 commentary; also Noren Drug Saf 2026. Only the empirical same-system comparison is left. MADE itself evaluates on a 'truncated test set' made by stratified sampling, after HDBSCAN downsampling that keeps a high share of rare labels (verified in the html). It is a ready example.

LLMs over-label in general: CatLLM (Soria 2026, abstract) reports this for 21 LLMs, with precision 40-50 points below sensitivity, and names definitions, unanimous ensembles and an 'Other' category as fixes. LLM-codex 2023 shows the same for ICD. Per-class fixes can work at web scale (Caswell: median precision 5.5% to 71.2% with tunable wordlists), and LoRA cut false positives at 0.35% prevalence (Liao 2026). 'No fix works' must be scoped.

Certifying per-unit precision needs tens to hundreds of calibration examples per unit (Available Guardrails arXiv 2609.22048: 179 for one group, 450 each for fifty, floor 29). 'No rule can auto-accept codes with 1-5 reports' follows from known arithmetic and should be cited as such.

Ranked read-first lists are two-phase TAR (Yang, Lewis & Frieder 2021; Cochrane RCT classifier; Bron 2024). TAR has been run on single categories down to about 0.2% prevalence (RCV1 I24000 at 0.002133). Many-category e-discovery where the reader also assigns the category exists (Harbison et al. CEUR 2024: 70 requests grouped into 10 CAL reviews). So does multiclass rare-item search (Nguyen & Garnett; Hartford et al. NeurIPS 2020). The list is not a method contribution.

LLM coding of MAUDE device-problem codes: Li H et al. npj Digit Med 2026 (487 IMDRF codes; judges preferred the LLM's code in 60.8 of 90 reports, the filer's in 21.7). Muaz et al. IFIP AIAI 2026 (snippet only). An LLM assigning NEISS product codes: Circo blog, May 2025 (gpt-4o-mini plus a retriever, 500 cases from 2024, 66.40%, scored as a match to any of Product_1-3). I re-opened the blog. The first-round critic was wrong on this.

Temporal split plus natural-frequency test over thousands of codes with a fine-tuned generative coder: Coutinho et al. PLOS Digit Health 2026. Macro precision is about 21% at about 80% accuracy; they also test a later period. There is no rare-code false-positive count and no zero-shot LLM.

map.claim2_split:
Claim 2 is taken as a finding and now on our own data source. MADE (ACL 2026) shows the same split on openFDA device reports, with a temporal split, frequency bins and a retrieval-prompted LLM given 10 kNN examples. Fine-tuned LLMs up to 70B do not close the extreme-tail gap. Motzfeldt, Yock/Eng, Martin/Feng/Peng, Emer, Zhou 2023 and Kaehler 2026 repeat it elsewhere. Li Z 2512.21041 (12 codes) found no LLM advantage on rare codes, and FLAN-FinXC and Al Monsur show LoRA helping the tail. So 'LoRA does not close the gap' is a finding for our data, not a rule.

Two pieces are still unreported:
- the training-size sweep of the encoder against a fixed LLM, reported per frequency bin;
- the 1-5-training-report bin, which MADE excludes by its 5-occurrence minimum.

Nothing new needs to be run: the sweep exists. In the paper, claim 2 should become supporting evidence that cites MADE first, with the sweep as its one new element. It is not a headline contribution.
map.claim3_natural:
Part of claim 3 is taken: the base-rate collapse in principle, the general LLM over-labelling, and the arithmetic that per-code certification is impossible. Caswell 2020 makes the balanced-test argument over up to 1,629 classes. Chen 2026 and Noren 2026 make it for LLMs. CatLLM 2026 reports over-labelling by 21 LLMs. Available Guardrails gives the certification counts. The phrase 'no fix works' is also contradicted in other settings: wordlist filters in Caswell, LoRA in Liao, definitions and unanimity in CatLLM.

What remains new, and still unreported after about 50 queries in this round (with OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar down):
- the measured per-code and pooled false-naming rate of zero-shot and retrieval LLM coders over hundreds of codes at about 0.08%, tested on a held-out year;
- the failure of the specific fixes tried;
- the coverage ceiling (219 of 552);
- the read-first list as an operating point. TAR stops at about 0.2% single-category prevalence, so the claim is the pooled 0.08% multi-code band with code naming, not the list as a method.

Deciding experiments, all cheap and CPU-only on existing outputs:
- (1) Score the same coders under natural, stratified (MADE/Yock-style) and balanced protocols and report rare-code precision under each. This turns the general argument into a measurement.
- (2) Add the fixes reviewers will name: per-code keyword/wordlist filters with a precision knob, CatLLM-style definitions with unanimity, and candidate restriction.
- (3) Audit a sample of 'false' rare answers for label noise (Li H).
- (4) Run TAR baselines on the list: per-code TF-IDF two-phase, simulated CAL, conformal selection. Also give either a stopping rule or the infeasibility arithmetic.
map.best_contribution: Best: On two report streams coded by their filers, a whole later year scored at natural proportions changes the picture that stratified tests give. Rare-code reports are about 1 in 1,200. A zero-shot or retrieval-prompted LLM names a rare code on 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports, so nearly all its rare-code answers are false. The fixes we tried do not change this on a held-out year, and only 219 of 552 rare reports are reached by any coder. The same coders scored under stratified and balanced protocols look far better (once that comparison is run). What does work at this prevalence is a frozen ranked read-first list: it finds 200 of 552 rare reports in about 7,000 reads, against about 16,000 for the encoder alone. Second best: a per-coder selector frozen on the training year chooses among an encoder, a zero-shot LLM and a retrieval LLM after all have answered, using mainly the training support of each proposed code. It adds 0.03 to 0.06 macro-F1 over the best single coder on later years, across two datasets and three LLMs, and beats confidence cascades, majority vote and (to be shown) energy-based routing and a per-code precision table.

map.plain_summary: The "LLMs win on rare codes, the trained model wins on common codes" result has been shown before, now even on FDA device reports by a 2026 paper called MADE. Treat it as backing, not as news, and cite MADE prominently. The selector is still not published in our form, but two ideas in it are: routing between models, and using how rare the proposed code is. EnergyRoute does the routing on about 300 classes with a later-year test, and a 2025 education paper sends rare-code answers to people. So the selector is an increment, and it needs a few more baselines (energy routing, a per-code precision table, the simple rare-code rule, and the selector without its count input) to prove the count adds something. The strongest new part is the natural-proportion measurement: how often LLMs falsely name rare codes at about 1 in 1,000, that our fixes did not help, and that only 219 of 552 rare reports are reached at all. The general idea that balanced tests flatter rare-class precision is old (a 2020 language-ID paper), so we must show it with numbers on our own coders by scoring them three ways. Reviewers will ask why we did not try keyword filters per code and longer code definitions, which helped elsewhere. Some of our "false" rare answers may be correct, because an FDA-linked study found judges often prefer an LLM's code over the filer's. The read-first list is standard review practice; what is new is the very low rate (0.08%) pooled over hundreds of codes. NEISS is still the best extra dataset and has a 2025 file, but someone already tried an LLM on its product codes in a blog post. No other country's report data were usable. Still unsure: three closed 2026 papers in our target journal (Hou, Ding, Chhetri) could not be read, and two of the big search services were blocked this round, so "nobody has done this" is a medium-confidence statement.

critic.verdict:
Most of the map is supported by the follow-up reports. I opened three claims myself (MADE, Li Z, EnergyRoute) and they mostly hold. One decisive claim is wrong. The map says TAR "stops at about 0.2%" single-category prevalence, so only the band below is unstudied. The paper that defines those RCV1 bins (Yang, Lewis, Frieder et al., arXiv 2106.09866) sets its "Rare" bin at 500-2,000 positive documents out of 804,414, which is about 0.06% to 0.25%. That bin covers our 0.08%, and the map's 0.002133 figure is only one example category inside it. It is the "extremely low" bin below 500 positives that was left out. So the read-first list's novelty has to rest on pooling hundreds of codes, naming the code, and the frozen later year, not on the prevalence band.

The map also overstates two points from Li Z 2512.21041:
- It says that paper found no LLM advantage on rare codes. In fact GPT-4o beat BERT on 4 rare codes where BERT scored 0.00, and lost on 4 others.
- It describes the routed path as "GPT-4o adjudication" and later as "goes to the LLM". In fact GPT-4o only suggests codes, and human experts make the decision.
