errors: Map (taken, ranking; open item 4; claim3_natural) says TAR has been run on single categories 'down to about 0.2% prevalence' and that 'TAR stops at about 0.2%'. Wrong. Yang, Lewis, Frieder et al. (arXiv 2106.09866; PDF text read) bin RCV1-v2 categories by number of positive documents: Rare is 500-2,000 of 804,414 documents, about 0.06%-0.25%. Only the 'Too rare' bin (<500) was dropped. The 0.002133 category (I24000) is one example inside the Rare bin, not its floor. The same authors' stopping-rules paper (2106.09871) describes the same 9-bin design, so its Rare categories can also sit near 0.08%. I did not confirm its bin limits directly. Single-category TAR at our pooled prevalence is therefore published.

Map claim2_split says 'Li Z 2512.21041 (12 codes) found no LLM advantage on rare codes'. The paper's pre-optimisation table (html read) gives GPT-4o above BERT on four rare codes: CK 0.25 vs 0.00, SR 0.19 vs 0.00, RT 0.13 vs 0.00, OS 0.11 vs 0.00. BERT is higher on PQ, RR, SI and FQ. The overall conclusion is that LLMs did not beat BERT, but the per-code picture is mixed and partly supports claim 2. The venue report's 'kappa near zero for both on most of them' was carried over without checking.

Map (taken, item 3) says routed items go to 'an expert, with GPT-4o adjudication', and claim1 baseline (c) says 'rare-code-or-low-confidence goes to the LLM'. In the paper, GPT-4o only proposes candidate codes and rationales. Human experts adjudicate, and GPT-4o's suggestions were 'not accepted automatically'. Baseline (c) is therefore an adaptation and should be called one.

Map (taken, MADE) says GPT-5 'roughly doubles the best fine-tuned model'. That holds only against generative Llama-70B (0.16). The best discriminative models are lower: Ettin-1B encoder 0.13 and Llama-8B 0.12 (MADE Table 2, read). Also, the MADE abstract itself says smaller discriminatively fine-tuned decoders give the strongest head-to-tail accuracy. A reviewer will quote that abstract, so the map should state MADE's own headline alongside the extreme-tail result.

Map (taken, item 5) says MADE's HDBSCAN downsampling 'keeps a high share of rare labels (verified in the html)'. The html says this, but it never measures it or names the stratification variables. The tail agent explicitly could not confirm how the stratification was done. 'Verified' should read 'stated by the authors'.
overclaims: Claim 1's 'what remains new' leans on the decision being made 'after all three coders have answered'. Stacking and meta-learners over finished outputs already do this: AspectBench's linear and random-forest stackers and complete LLM deferral (the LLM sees the expert's label), LabelFusion, and LAVA's meta-learner ensembles of GPT-5 and classifiers (abstract read; method not described). The map's 'every published router decides before the LLM answers' is true of routers, not of stackers. The increment is the support feature, learned per coder, frozen, at natural proportions.

LAVA (arXiv 2509.09602) was listed as unverified by the selector agent and then dropped from the map entirely. Its meta-learner could be a post-answer selector between an LLM and classifiers. This is unresolved and should stay on the must-read list.

The map says 'Claim 2 is a replication, except for the per-bin training-size sweep'. The first-round critic asked for 'mostly replicated'. MADE is multi-label with ancestor labels, drops labels with fewer than 5 occurrences, and is scored on a stratified truncated test. Our 1-5-report single-label bin at natural proportions is therefore not covered. The map lists these under open items but phrases the headline flatly.

The map's statement that 'no rule can auto-accept codes with 1-5 reports follows from known arithmetic' treats Available Guardrails' certification counts (179, 450 and 29, abstract and full text read by the ranking agent, not by me) as if they explained our empirical failure. Certifying precision with a guarantee and a rule failing empirically are different claims. The paper should cite the arithmetic for the first and keep its own measurement for the second.
